# LINEAR ALGEBRAIC METHOD AND THE ERD ̋S-HEILBRONN CONJECTURE

GUANZHONG YANG

Abstract. Additive combinatorics asks for lower bounds on sumsets and restricted sumsets over finite fields. Central examples are the Cauchy–Davenport theorem and the Erd ̋os–Heilbronn conjecture. In this note, we develop Das’s linear algebraic method and give a new elementary proof of the Alon–Nathanson–Ruzsa theorem for restricted sumsets, which implies the Erd ̋os–Heilbronn conjecture. Compared with the classical polynomial method via Combinatorial Nullstellensatz, our proof uses only basic linear algebra over finite fields, including Vandermonde matrices and solvability of linear systems.

### 1. Introduction

Additive combinatorics is a central branch of combinatorial number theory, focusing on the additive structure of subsets of integers and finite fields [7]. A foundational problem in this field is to give sharp lower bounds for the cardinality of sumsets, which has wide applications in number theory, combinatorics, and theoretical computer science.

Let _p_ be a prime number, and let Z_/p_Z denote the finite field of integers modulo _p_. For nonempty subsets _A,B_ of Z_/p_Z, the classical sumset is defined as

\(A+B=\{a+b:a\in A,b\in B\}.\)

The celebrated Cauchy-Davenport theorem, a cornerstone of additive combinatorics, gives a tight lower bound for the size of such sumsets:

\(|A+B|\unknown min\{p,|A|+|B|-1\}.\)

In 1964, Erd ̋os and Heilbronn proposed a famous conjecture for the so-called restricted sumset, where the summands are required to be distinct [5]. For nonempty subsets _A,B_ of Z_/p_Z, we define the restricted sumset as

\(A\dot{+}B=\{a+b:a\in A,b\in B,a\neq b\}.\)

arXiv:2605.19542v1 [math.CO] 19 May 2026

<tbc>The Erdős-Heilbronn conjecture states that for any nonempty subset _A_ of Z_/p_Z,<tbc>

\(|A\dot{+}A|\ge min\{p,2|A|-3\}.\)

<tbc>This conjecture remained open for 30 years, until it was first proven by Dias da Silva and Hamidoune in 1994, using tools from exterior algebra and representation theory [4]. In 1995, Alon, Nathanson and Ruzsa developed the polynomial method, specifically the Combinatorial Nullstellensatz [2, 1], to give a simpler proof of a more general result: for nonempty subsets _A,B_ of Z_/p_Z with \(|A|\neq|B|\),

\(|A\dot{+}B|\ge min\{p,|A|+|B|-2\}.\)

This general result directly implies the original Erdős-Heilbronn conjecture as a corollary.

In the decades since, multiple new proofs of the Cauchy-Davenport theorem and the Erdős-Heilbronn conjecture have been developed, using tools ranging from harmonic analysis to the uncertainty principle on finite cyclic groups [6]. In 2004, Das introduced a linear algebraic method to give a new proof of the Cauchy-Davenport theorem, relying only on elementary linear algebra over finite fields [3]. In this note, we extend Das’s linear algebraic approach to give a new, elementary proof of the Alon-Nathanson-Ruzsa theorem for restricted sumsets. Compared with existing proofs, our method requires no advanced algebraic or combinatorial machinery, only standard undergraduate-level linear algebra, including Vandermonde matrices and the solvability of linear systems over finite fields.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 collects the preliminary definitions and auxiliary lemmas that form the foundation of our proof. Section 3 states our main results, including the main theorem and its direct corollary, the Erdős-Heilbronn theorem. The complete proof of the main theorem is presented in Section 4. We conclude with some brief remarks and directions for future work in Section 5.

## 2. Preliminaries

In this section, we introduce the core definitions and auxiliary lemmas used throughout the paper. All sets are assumed to be nonempty subsets of Z_/p_Z, where _p_ is a fixed prime number. For a finite set _S_, we write |_S_| for the cardinality (number of elements) of _S_.

Let _A_={_a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a<sub>m</sub>_} be a subset of Z_/p_Z with _a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a<sub>m</sub>_ pairwise distinct. Let _w(a_<sub>1</sub>)_,...,w(a<sub>m</sub>_) be a sequence in Z_/p_Z satisfying \(w(a_\ell)\) is nonzero in Z_/p_Z for some \(1\le\ell\le m\). We shall say a sequence

<tbc>_u_<sub>1</sub>_,...,u<sub>n</sub>_ a nonzero sequence if \(u_\ell\neq 0\) for some \(1\le\ell\le n\). We use _e<sub>A</sub>(w_) to denote the smallest natural number _i_ such that \(\sum_{j=1}^mw(a_j)a_j^i\) is nonzero in Z_/p_Z. We have the following conclusion.

**Lemma 2.1.** _Let A, w and e<sub>A</sub>(w_) _be as above. Then_<tbc>

\(e_A(w)\le|A|-1.\)

<tbc>_Proof._ It is proved by contradiction. Suppose that \(e_A(w)\ge|A|\). This means

\(\sum_{j=1}^mw(a_j)a_j^i=0\) (2.1)

for all \(0\le i\le m-1\).

The (coefficients) matrix _M_ is defined to be<tbc>

\(M=(a_j^{i-1})_{1\le i\le m}.\) (2.2)

<tbc>Note that<tbc>

\(det(M)=\prod_{1\le i<j\le m}(a_j-a_i).\)

<tbc>Since _a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a<sub>m</sub>_ are pairwise distinct in Z_/p_Z, det(_M_) is nonzero. Consider the system of linear equations

\(M\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0},\) (2.3)

where **x**=(_x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>m</sub>)<sup>T</sup>_ and **0**=(0_,...,_0)_<sup>T</sup>_.

On one hand, (2.3) has only the zero solution due to the fact that det(_M_) is nonzero. On the other hand, (_w(a_<sub>1</sub>)_,...,w(a<sub>m</sub>_))_<sup>T</sup>_ is a solution to (2.3) in view of (2.1). This is a contradiction since \(w(a_\ell)\) is nonzero in Z_/p_Z for some \(1\le\ell\le m\). This completes the proof. □

The inequality in Lemma 2.1 is sharp since we have the following.

**Lemma 2.2.** _Let A_={_a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a<sub>m</sub>_} _be a subset of_ Z_/p_Z _with_ \(m\ge 2\)_. Then there exists a nonzero sequence w(a_<sub>1</sub>)_,...,w(a<sub>m</sub>_) _such that_<tbc>

\(e_A(w)=|A|-1.\)

<tbc>_Proof._ The proof is similar to that of Lemma 2.1. Let _M_ be as in (2.2). Now consider the linear equations

\(M\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},\) (2.4)

where **x**=(_x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>m</sub>)<sup>T</sup>_ and **b**=(0_,...,_0,1)_<sup>T</sup>_. Since det(_M_) is nonzero, (2.4) has a unique solution (_w_<sub>1</sub>_,...,w<sub>m</sub>)<sup>T</sup>_. Since **b** is a nonzero vector, (_w_<sub>1</sub>_,...,w<sub>m</sub>)<sup>T</sup>_ is also a nonzero vector. In particular, we have

\(w_\ell\) is nonzero for some \(1\le\ell\le m\). On choosing _w(aj_)=_wj_ for \(1\le j\le m\), we have \(\sum_{j=1}^mw(a_j)a_j^i=0\) for all \(0\le i\le m-2\), and \(\sum_{j=1}^mw(a_j)a_j^{m-1}=1.\) According to the definition of _eA(w_), we have _eA(w_)=_m_-1=|_A_|-1. This completes the proof. □ ## 3. Main Results In this section, we state our main results, including the general lower bound for restricted sumsets (the Alon-Nathanson-Ruzsa theorem) and its direct corollary, the Erdős-Heilbronn theorem. We continue to work over the finite field Z_/p_Z for a fixed prime _p_, with all sumset notation consistent with Section 1. **Theorem 3.1** (Main Theorem)**.** _Let A and B be nonempty subsets of_ Z_/p_Z _with_ \(|A|\neq|B|\)_. Then the cardinality of the restricted sumset satisfies_ \(|A\dot{+}B|\ge min\{p,|A|+|B|-2\}.\) This main theorem directly implies the classical Erdős-Heilbronn conjecture, which we state formally as a corollary below. **Corollary 3.1** (Erdős-Heilbronn Theorem)**.** _Let A be a nonempty subset of_ Z_/p_Z_. Then_ \(|A\dot{+}A|\ge min\{p,2|A|-3\}.\) _Proof._ Fix any element \(a_0\in A\), and define \(A'=A\backslash\{a_0\}\). Then \(|A|\neq|A'|\), and it is straightforward to verify that \(A\dot{+}A=A\dot{+}A'\): any sum _a+b_ with \(a,b\in A\) and \(a\neq b\) can be written as a sum of an element from _A_ and an element from \(A'\) with distinct summands, and vice versa. Applying the Main Theorem to the pair \((A,A')\), we get \(|A\dot{+}A|=|A\dot{+}A'|\ge min\{p,|A|+|A'|-2\}\)
\(=min\{p,|A|+(|A|-1)-2\}\)
\(=min\{p,2|A|-3\},\) which completes the proof. □

<tbc>Our proof of the Main Theorem, presented in the next section, uses only the elementary linear algebraic tools established in Section 2. This gives a more accessible proof of the Erd ́os-Heilbronn theorem, avoiding the advanced combinatorial and algebraic machinery used in prior arguments.

## 4. Proof of the Main Theorem

In this section, we give the complete proof of the Main Theorem using the linear algebraic tools from Section 2. We split the proof into several auxiliary lemmas, followed by the final argument for the main result.

Let _A_={_a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a<sub>m</sub>_} and _B_={_b_<sub>1</sub>_,...,b<sub>k</sub>_} be subsets of Z_/p_Z. Let _w_<sub>1</sub>(_a_<sub>1</sub>)_,...,w_<sub>1</sub>(_a<sub>m</sub>_) and _w_<sub>2</sub>(_b_<sub>1</sub>)_,...,w_<sub>2</sub>(_b<sub>k</sub>_) be two sequences in Z_/p_Z. For nonnegative integer _i_, we introduce

\(\alpha_i:=\alpha_i(A,w_1)=\sum_{j=1}^mw_1(a_j)a_j^i\) (4.5)

and

\(\beta_i:=\beta_i(B,w_2)=\sum_{j=1}^kw_2(b_j)b_j^i.\) (4.6)

Let \(C=A\dot{+}B\), and suppose that _C_={_c_<sub>1</sub>_,...,c<sub>t</sub>_}. For \(c_j\in C\), we define<tbc>

\(w(c_j)=\sum_{a\in A,b\in Ba+b=c_j}w_1(a)w_2(b)(a-b).\)

<tbc>Then we introduce

\(\gamma_i:=\gamma_i(C,w)=\sum_{j=1}^tw(c_j)c_j^i.\)

**Lemma 4.1.** _Let A,B,C and_ \(\alpha_i,\beta_i,\gamma_i\) _be as above. Then_

\(\gamma_n=\sum_{i=0}^nC_n^i\alpha_{i+1}\beta_{n-i}-\sum_{i=0}^nC_n^i\alpha_i\beta_{n+1-i}.\)

_Proof._ Note that \(\gamma_n=\sum_{j=1}^tw(c_j)c_j^n=\sum_{j=1}^tc_j^n\sum_{a\in A,b\in Ba+b=c_j}w_1(a)w_2(b)(a-b)\)
\(=\sum_{a\in A,b\in B}w_1(a)w_2(b)(a-b)(a+b)^n.\) Since \((a+b)^n=\sum_{i=0}^nC_n^ia^ib^{n-i},\) we have \(\gamma_n=\sum_{a\in A,b\in B}w_1(a)w_2(b)(a-b)\sum_{i=0}^nC_n^ia^ib^{n-i}\)
\(=\sum_{a\in A,b\in B}w_1(a)w_2(b)\sum_{i=0}^nC_n^ia^{i+1}b^{n-i}\)
\(-\sum_{a\in A,b\in B}w_1(a)w_2(b)\sum_{i=0}^nC_n^ia^ib^{n+1-i}.\) We observe that \(\sum_{a\in A,b\in B}w_1(a)w_2(b)\sum_{i=0}^nC_n^ia^{i+1}b^{n-i}\)
\(=\sum_{i=0}^nC_n^i\big(\sum_{a\in A}w_1(a)a^{i+1}\big)\big(\sum_{b\in B}w_2(b)b^{n-i}\big)\)
\(=\sum_{i=0}^nC_n^i\alpha_{i+1}\beta_{n-i}.\) Similarly, we also have \(\sum_{a\in A,b\in B}w_1(a)w_2(b)\sum_{i=0}^nC_n^ia^ib^{n+1-i}\)
\(=\sum_{i=0}^nC_n^i\big(\sum_{a\in A}w_1(a)a^i\big)\big(\sum_{b\in B}w_2(b)b^{n+1-i}\big)\)
\(=\sum_{i=0}^nC_n^i\alpha_i\beta_{n+1-i}.\)

<tbc>Now we can conclude from above that

\(\gamma_n=\sum_{i=0}^nC_n^i\alpha_{i+1}\beta_{n-i}-\sum_{i=0}^nC_n^i\alpha_i\beta_{n+1-i}.\)

The proof of this lemma is finished. □

**Lemma 4.2.** _Let A,B,C and_ \(\alpha_i,\beta_i,\gamma_i\) _be as above. Let r,s be non- negative integers. Assume that_ \(\alpha_i=0\) _for_ \(0\le i\le r\) _and_ \(\beta_i=0\) _for_ \(0\le i\le s\)_. Then_<tbc>

\(\gamma_{r+s+1}=\big(C_{r+s+1}^r-C_{r+s+1}^s\big)\alpha_{r+1}\beta_{s+1}\)

<tbc>_and_<tbc>

\(\gamma_n=0\text{\textit{for all}}0\le n\le r+s.\)

<tbc>_Proof._ By Lemma 4.1,<tbc>

\(\gamma_{r+s+1}=\sum_{i=0}^{r+s+1}C_{r+s+1}^i\alpha_{i+1}\beta_{r+s+1-i}-\sum_{i=0}^{r+s+1}C_{r+s+1}^i\alpha_i\beta_{r+s+2-i}.\)

<tbc>If \(i\le r-1\), then \(i+1\le r\) and thus \(\alpha_{i+1}=0\). If \(i\ge r+1\), then \(r+s+1-i\le s\) and thus \(\beta_{r+s+1-i}=0\). Therefore, \(\alpha_{i+1}\beta_{r+s+1-i}=0\) for all \(i\neq r\). Then we have<tbc>

\(\sum_{i=0}^{r+s+1}C_{r+s+1}^i\alpha_{i+1}\beta_{r+s+1-i}=C_{r+s+1}^r\alpha_{r+1}\beta_{s+1}.\)

<tbc>Similarly, \(\alpha_i\beta_{r+s+2-i}=0\) for all \(i\neq r+1\). Then we have<tbc>

\(\sum_{i=0}^{r+s+1}C_{r+s+1}^i\alpha_i\beta_{r+s+2-i}=C_{r+s+1}^s\alpha_{r+1}\beta_{s+1}.\)

<tbc>We conclude from above<tbc>

\(\gamma_{r+s+1}=\big(C_{r+s+1}^r-C_{r+s+1}^s\big)\alpha_{r+1}\beta_{s+1}.\)

<tbc>We have

\(\gamma_n=\sum_{i=0}^nC_n^i\alpha_{i+1}\beta_{n-i}-\sum_{i=0}^nC_n^i\alpha_i\beta_{n+1-i}.\)

For \(n\le r+s\), we have \((i+1)+(n-i)=n+1\le r+s+1\). Then either \(i+1\le r\) or \(n-i\le s\). Thus, \(\alpha_{i+1}\beta_{n-i}=0\) for all \(0\le i\le n\). Similarly, \(\alpha_i\beta_{n+1-i}=0\) for all \(0\le i\le n\). Then we conclude that \(\gamma_n=0\) for \(n\le r+s\).

The proof of this lemma is finished. □

**Lemma 4.3.** _Suppose that_ |_A_|=1 _or_ |_B_|=1_. Then_

\(|A\dot{+}B|\ge min\{p,|A|+|B|-2\}.\)

<tbc>_Proof._ Without loss of generality, we can assume that |_A_|=1. If |_B_|=1, then the desired inequality holds trivially (although it is possible that \(A\dot{+}B=\emptyset\)). Now we consider the case \(|B|\ge 2\). We write _A_={_a_<sub>0</sub>} and |_B_|=_k_. We can find _k_-1 distinct elements _b_<sub>1</sub>_,...,b_<sub>_k_-1</sub> in _B_ such that \(b_i\neq a_0\) for \(1\le i\le k-1\).

Note that \(a_0+b_1,\dots,a_0+b_{k-1}\in A\dot{+}B\). Thus, \(|A\dot{+}B|\ge k-1=|A|+|B|-2=min\{p,|A|+|B|-2\}\). The proof of this lemma is finished.

□

Now we are able to prove the Main Theorem. If \(|A|+|B|-2\ge p+1\), we claim that there exist nonempty subsets \(A'\subset A\) and \(B'\subset B\) such that \(|A'|+|B'|-2=p\) and \(|A'|\neq|B'|\).

Suppose that |_A_|+|_B_|-2=_p+d_ with \(d\ge 1\). We write \(d_1=\lfloor d/2\rfloor\) and \(d_2=\lceil d/2\rceil\). Clearly, _d_<sub>1</sub>+_d_<sub>2</sub>=_d_. Without loss of generality, we assume that |_A|\<|B_|. We choose _d_<sub>2</sub> elements \(a'_1,\dots,a'_{d_2}\) in _A_ and _d_<sub>1</sub> elements \(b'_1,\dots,b'_{d_1}\) in _B_. Let \(A'=A\backslash\{a'_1,\dots,a'_{d_2}\}\) and \(B'=B\backslash\{b'_1,\dots,b'_{d_1}\}\). From \(|A|+|B|-2=p+d\), we can see that \(|A|\ge d+2\ge d_2+2\). Thus, \(A'\) is nonempty and \(|A'|=|A|-d_2\). Similarly, \(B'\) is nonempty and \(|B'|=|B|-d_1\). We have \(|A'|<|B'|\) since |_A|\<|B_| and \(d_2\ge d_1\). It is easy to check that \(|A'|+|B'|-2=|A|-d_2+|B|-d_1-2=|A|+|B|-2-d=p\). Therefore, the above claim is true.

Now it suffices to prove the Main Theorem in the case \(|A|+|B|-2\le p\), since if \(|A|+|B|-2\ge p+1\) then \(|A\dot{+}B|\ge|A'\dot{+}B'|\ge min\{p,|A'|+|B'|-2\}=p=min\{p,|A|+|B|-2\}\).

From now on, we assume that \(|A|+|B|-2\le p\). Let _A_={_a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a<sub>m</sub>_} and _B_={_b_<sub>1</sub>_,...,b<sub>k</sub>_}. We have \(m+k\le p+2\). In view of Lemma 4.3, we can assume that \(m\ge 2\) and \(k\ge 2\). Let _C=A_\(\dot{+}B=\{c_1,\dots,c_t\}\). By Lemma 2.2, there exists a nonzero sequence _w_<sub>1</sub>(_a_<sub>1</sub>)_,...,w_<sub>1</sub>(_a<sub>m</sub>_) such that

\(e_A(w_1)=|A|-1=m-1.\) (4.7)

Also, there exists a nonzero sequence _w_<sub>2</sub>(_b_<sub>1</sub>)_,...,w_<sub>2</sub>(_b<sub>k</sub>_) such that

\(e_B(w_2)=|B|-1=k-1.\) (4.8)

Recalling the definitions of \(\alpha_i:=\alpha_i(A,w_1)\) and \(\beta_i:=\beta_i(B,w_2)\), we conclude from (4.7) and (4.8) that \(\alpha_i=0\) for \(0\le i\le m-2\), \(\alpha_{m-1}\neq 0\), \(\beta_i=0\) for \(0\le i\le k-2\) and \(\beta_{k-1}\neq 0\).

Applying Lemma 4.2 with _r=m_-2 and _s=k_-2, we obtain

\(\gamma_{m+k-3}=\big(C_{m+k-3}^{m-2}-C_{m+k-3}^{k-2}\big)\alpha_{m-1}\beta_{k-1}.\)

<tbc>Since \(m+k-3\le p-1\) and \(m\neq k\), we have \(C_{m+k-3}^{m-2}-C_{m+k-3}^{k-2}\unknown=0(modp)\). Note that \(\alpha_{m-1}\beta_{k-1}\) is nonzero, we have \(\gamma_{m+k-3}\neq 0\). By Lemma 4.2, we also have \(\gamma_n=0\) for \(0\le n\le m+k-4\).

Therefore, _m+k_-3 is the smallest natural number _i_ such that \(\sum_{j=1}^tw(c_j)c_j^i\) is nonzero. According to the definition of _e<sub>C</sub>(w_), we have _e<sub>C</sub>(w_)=_m+k_-3.

We apply Lemma 2.1 to the set _C_ to conclude that \(e_C(w)\le|C|-1\). Now we obtain \(|C|\ge e_C(w)+1=m+k-2\). This proves \(|A+\dagger B|\ge|A|+|B|-2=min\{p,|A|+|B|-2\}\). The proof of the Main Theorem is finished.

## 5. Concluding Remarks

In this note, we developed the linear algebraic method initiated by Das to give a new, elementary proof of the Alon-Nathanson-Ruzsa theorem for restricted sumsets, which directly implies the classical Erdős- Heilbronn conjecture. Unlike prior proofs that rely on the Combinatorial Nullstellensatz, exterior algebra, or harmonic analysis, our argument uses only standard undergraduate linear algebra over finite fields, making the result more accessible to a broader audience.

There are several natural directions for future work. First, it would be interesting to extend this linear algebraic approach to more general restricted sumset results, for example the Dias da Silva-Hamidoune theorem for sums of _n_ distinct elements. Second, our method is currently restricted to sumsets over finite fields of prime order. It remains open whether this framework can be adapted to give lower bounds for sumsets over composite moduli or more general abelian groups. Finally, this approach may have applications to other problems in additive combinatorics, such as the Erdős-Szemerédi theorem on sum-product sets, which we leave for future investigation.
